title: Your opinion, your reasons
goal: Say what you think. Give two different reasons. Back up each reason with a real example.

card.title: FOUR BOXES
lines: Box 1: OPINION + 2 REASONS. 'I think … because … and …'
Box 2: REASON 1 + a little more about it + a real EXAMPLE + why it matters. 'One reason is … For example, … This shows …'
Box 3: REASON 2, the same way. 'Another reason is …'
Box 4: 'In conclusion, …' Say your opinion and both reasons again, in short. Then add one ending sentence. No new reasons.
A real example gives at least two of these: who exactly, what exactly, when, how much.
Reason menu (kinds of reasons): money · time · sleep and health · safety · learning · friends and family · stress and fun · fairness · the future.

same.label: the same reason again
same.feedback: That is the same reason in different words.

vague.label: still vague
vague.feedback: That is still vague. Who exactly? When? How much?

reason.label: a reason, not an example
reason.feedback: That is a new reason, not an example. A real example is a real case, with a who, a when or a how much.

later.title: Should high schools start later in the morning?
sentences: I think high schools should start later in the morning, because teenagers need more sleep and because students learn more when they are awake.
One reason is that teenagers need more sleep.
Many students stay up late doing homework or working, and then they have to be up at 6:30 to catch the bus.
For example, my friend works until 10 p.m. on weeknights and is half asleep in first period.
If school started at 9:30, he would get one more hour of sleep and could actually pay attention.
Another reason is that students would learn more.
It is hard to understand math at 8:00 a.m. when your brain is not awake yet.
Last year my first-period class was science, and when the same class moved to the afternoon, my marks went up.
This shows that the time of day changes how much students learn.
In conclusion, schools should start later because students would get more sleep and do better in class.
It is a small change that would make a big difference.
later.tutorNote: A model essay, not a reading passage. Each paragraph is one of the four boxes.

sections.title: Four boxes
sections.tutorNote: I DO. Read the four boxes. Reveal the model essay one box at a time and name each part aloud: opinion and two reasons; reason, a little more about it, a real example, why it matters; again; conclusion and one closing sentence. Then the student taps the side the writer is on and each real example. Point out that the opinion is the same at the start and at the end.

text: An opinion essay has four boxes. Each box is one paragraph.
Box 1: what you think, and your two reasons.
Box 2: reason one, a real example, and why it matters.
Box 3: reason two, a real example, and why it matters.
Box 4: say your opinion and reasons again, in short. Add one ending sentence.
A real example gives at least two of these: who exactly, what exactly, when, how much.

sections.title: Make it real
sections.tutorNote: WE DO: the vague-to-specific drill. Say the vague version; the student makes it real by adding who exactly, what exactly, when and how much. Push with 'Who exactly? When? How much?' An example is a real case, not another reason. The typed examples go to the review queue; score 0 to 2. Any real detail is fine; it does not have to match the model, and it may be made up if it could be real.

text: A reason needs a real example.
'Phones are distracting' is vague. That means it could be about anyone, at any time.
'My phone buzzed in math and I missed the homework' is real.
A real example gives at least two of these: who exactly, what exactly, when, how much.
Use you or someone you know. If you have no example, make up one that could be real.

WHY IT MATTERS: 'This shows…'

sections.title: First essay: four boxes
sections.tutorNote: YOU DO: the first whole essay, with the four boxes and their sentence starters. About five minutes to plan aloud or on paper, then about twenty to write; the timer is there if the student wants it. No help once the writing starts. Two marks, topic development and conventions, using my short summary of the test's own scoring guide, as a guide only. Note the word count, opinion first (yes or no), opinion kept (yes or no), the number of different reasons, of specific examples and of paragraphs. Then name ONE change that would move it up a level.

text: Write a whole essay.
Plan for about five minutes. Pick your side, two different reasons from the menu, and a real example for each.
Then write for about twenty minutes. Fill the four boxes in order.
Write it one time. Do not write a rough copy and then a good copy.

steps.stem: Should students be paid for good marks? Write an essay that gives your opinion and supports it with reasons and examples.

parts.label: Box 2: Reason 1, a real example, why it matters
Box 3: Reason 2, a real example, why it matters

checklist: I said my opinion in the first sentence.
It is the same opinion at the end.
I have two different reasons.
Each reason has a real example (who exactly, what exactly, when, how much).
There are four boxes (paragraphs).
It is over 150 words.
I read it out loud once. Every sentence ends with a period.
model: I think students should be paid for good marks because money makes students work harder and because it teaches them how to save.

One reason is that money makes students work harder. Many students do not see why a test matters, but they understand a reward. For example, my cousin's parents started paying him $20 for every mark over 80 last year, and he went from two marks over 80 to five. This shows that a small reward can change how hard a student tries.

Another reason is that it teaches students how to save. Teenagers do not get many chances to handle their own money. For example, my friend earned $60 for her report card in June and put half of it in the bank for a new bike. This shows that being paid for marks can teach a real money skill.
In conclusion, students should be paid for good marks because they would work harder and learn to save. It would be worth the cost.

steps.stem: Is it better to play on a team or to do a sport on your own? Write an essay that gives your opinion and supports it with reasons and examples.

parts.label: Box 1: Opinion and two reasons
parts.help: What you think, and your two reasons.

parts.label: Box 2: Reason 1, a real example, why it matters
parts.help: A reason, a little more about it, a real example, then why it matters.

parts.label: Box 3: Reason 2, a real example, why it matters
parts.help: A DIFFERENT reason, a little more about it, a real example, then why it matters.

parts.label: Box 4: In conclusion
parts.help: Your opinion and both reasons again, in short. Then one ending sentence. No new reasons.

checklist: I said my opinion in the first sentence.
It is the same opinion at the end.
I have two different reasons.
Each reason has a real example (who exactly, what exactly, when, how much).
There are four boxes (paragraphs).
It is over 150 words.
I read it out loud once. Every sentence ends with a period.
model: I think it is better to play on a team than to do a sport on your own because teammates make sure you come and because a team teaches you to work with other people.

One reason is that teammates make sure you come. When you train alone, it is easy to skip a day. For example, last winter I wanted to stay home from a 7 a.m. hockey practice, but two of my teammates texted me, so I went. This shows that a team keeps you going when you want to quit.

Another reason is that a team teaches you to work with other people. In a team sport, you cannot win by yourself. For example, in our last soccer game, I passed to a teammate instead of shooting, and she scored the winning goal. This shows that a team teaches you to trust others.
In conclusion, playing on a team is better because your teammates keep you going and you learn to work together. Those lessons last longer than the season.

sections.tutorNote: YOU DO: the mastery task. One box, no starters; the student starts a new line for each paragraph. The timer is set to twenty minutes, as in the plan. Guide threshold: two essays in a row on new prompts (the second essay and this one), each 150 words or more, with the opinion stated first and kept to the end, two different reasons, at least one specific example for each, four paragraphs, finished in 25 minutes, that you would mark Code 30 or higher for topic development.

Plan first. Pick your side, two different reasons, and a real example for each.
Start a new line for each of your four boxes (paragraphs).
Try to finish in about twenty minutes.

steps.stem: Should high school students have homework on weekends? Write an essay that gives your opinion and supports it with reasons and examples.
checklist: I said my opinion in the first sentence.
It is the same opinion at the end.
I have two different reasons.
Each reason has a real example (who exactly, what exactly, when, how much).
There are four paragraphs, each on a new line.
It is over 150 words.
I read it out loud once. Every sentence ends with a period.
model: I think high school students should not have homework on weekends because they need time to rest and because many of them work.

One reason is that students need time to rest. After five days of classes, the brain needs a break. For example, last month I had a history essay and a math sheet due on the same Monday, and I spent all of Sunday at my desk. This shows that weekend homework can leave students more tired on Monday than they were on Friday.

Another reason is that many students work on weekends. Two days are not enough for a long shift and a lot of homework. For example, my brother works at a restaurant from noon to eight every Saturday and does not start his homework until nine at night. This shows that weekend homework is hardest on students who have jobs.
In conclusion, students should not have homework on weekends because they need rest and many of them work. Two free days would send everyone back to school ready to learn.
